item.title: Can We Engineer Serendipity?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can We Engineer Serendipity?

Designing AI to find the unexpected changes the accident itself.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Serendipity requires both an unexpected observation and a mind prepared to recognize its significance.
  • AI can surface connections, but engineering the conditions for discovery changes the accident itself.
  • Once the unexpected is designed to be found, what remains may be useful but is no longer quite serendipity.
Source: Image by Angelo Esslinger from Pixabay.

I'll bet that Alexander Fleming wasn't thrilled to find mold growing in one of his laboratory dishes in 1928. Contamination generally isn't something scientists want or even celebrate.

But Fleming did notice something unusual. And I think that word is important. The bacteria surrounding the mold weren't growing. What he noticed helped give the world penicillin and transformed medicine. The zone of inhibition became a zone of discovery.

Fleming wasn't looking for penicillin; he was noticing something—something that wasn't supposed to be there at all. I wonder how many important scientific discoveries over time have emerged from that ability to see something new in what first appears to be a mistake or an irrelevant artifact.

About a hundred years earlier, Louis Pasteur offered an observation that nicely aligns with Fleming's observation: "In the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind." Clearly, Pasteur wasn't just celebrating luck; he was describing the dynamic between an observation and the ability to recognize the significance.

Today, artificial intelligence is adding an interesting twist to what is observed and interpreted. AI is becoming very good at finding answers, but as we move more "frictionlessly" from question to answer, I wonder what happens to the unexpected bumps we encounter (and might miss) along the way.

And there's another "evolving possibility" that is worth putting under the microscope: Could AI actually manufacture the conditions for serendipity?

The Things We Weren't Looking For

Let's jump back another one hundred years. The word serendipity was coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, based on a Persian tale called "The Three Princes of Serendip." In the story, the princes made discoveries through a combination of both accident and insight.

Serendipity isn't simply about finding something surprising—it's about finding something valuable that wasn't part of the plan.

I've written about "productive" cognitive friction and how the struggle (even confusion) can align with scientific discovery. The journey toward an answer can produce questions that are more interesting than the original problem. AI's efficiency may allow us to bypass some of those detours, along with the unexpected observations they occasionally reveal.

Now, back to Fleming. His mold wasn't an unexpected connection buried in a pile of data. It was an unexpected event living in our physical world. No one had asked for it, and it wasn't part of an academically approved study design. AI can uncover surprising relationships across wide and varied data sets, including connections a researcher might not recognize. But there's something different about an observation that arrives as an unexpected knock on the lab door, particularly when it challenges what we thought we knew.

The Prepared Machine?

After looking back a few hundred years, let's look at today.

A 2024 study in Science Advances found that generative AI helped individuals write stories that were judged to be more creative. So far so good. But creativity seemed to come at the expense of originality as the AI-assisted stories also became more similar. It's important to note that the study looked at creative writing rather than science, yet it might raise a related question. Could AI help each of us produce better ideas while potentially narrowing the diversity of ideas we explore?

A 2026 preprint from Princeton and the University of California, Berkeley, offers more recent perspective. The study explored if deliberately introducing ideas from unrelated topics could stimulate creativity in both humans and LLMs.

The results showed that humans consistently benefited from unexpected associations. But AI, which generally produced more original ideas in the study, showed no overall improvement from the added topics. It's my contention that AI's vast corpus of knowledge may not "incrementally" advance the "connectivity" as much of the information may already be contained in the training data.

So, here's my question: Can we deliberately engineer serendipity? And if we build AI to identify unexpected relationships, are there discoveries really serendipitous accidents? Or have we developed a more sophisticated method of searching?

I've written about a version of this idea in medicine with what I called an AI Zebra Scan. Rather than allowing AI to settle on the "most statistically probable diagnosis," why not design it to deliberately explore less likely possibilities? This isn't serendipity itself, but maybe it's a way to expand the range of possibilities that AI considers. And perhaps that same principle can be applied more broadly to scientific discovery.

  • Expand the hypothesis space. Explore possibilities beyond what's most probable.
  • Preserve anomalies. Investigate outlying observations rather than dismissing them as statistical noise.
  • Connect distant disciplines. Identify relationships outside established boundaries.
  • Challenge the original question. Consider if the assumptions themselves are limiting discovery.

Of course, these aren’t definitive rules for producing scientific breakthroughs. And they’re probably easier said than done. But there might be a few thought starters here for designing AI that could be receptive to the unexpected rather than simply optimizing the expected.

The Observer and the Observation

In the final analysis, there's a difference between discovering an unexpected relationship among things we know and the discovery of something that makes us to reconsider what we thought was even possible. Both can lead to discoveries, but they're not the same experience.

AI can do the first at scale. It can also be designed to notice anomalies and judge their significance. Once we deliberately create the conditions where the unexpected will be found and recognized, the accident is no longer accidental. In that sense, programming serendipity is a bit like Schrödinger’s cat—the act of looking for it changes what we find.

Pasteur’s "prepared mind" may be entering unfamiliar territory where AI increasingly participates in both the fortunate encounter and the judgment that turns it into a discovery. What remains may still be valuable. But is it really serendipity?

item.title: Fill-in-the-Consonants Puzzles
item.description:
Bias

Fill-in-the-Consonants Puzzles

The information entropy principle.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Puzzles like those on "Wheel of Fortune" are based on a communication principle known as information entropy.
  • Information entropy means, in a nutshell, that consonants carry more information than vowels.
  • The puzzles here aim to exemplify how the principle works.

In the American television quiz show "Wheel of Fortune," a contestant must guess a consonant missing from the words in a puzzle phrase for each spin of the wheel. But the contestant must pay $250 dollars from an accumulated amount of money to see what vowels are in the puzzle. The rules of the game are actually based on a well-known principle in linguistics and information theory that can be defined—in reference to the game itself—as the principle that it is easier to figure out what a word is if given only its consonants, but almost impossible to do so if given just its vowels.

Take, for example, the following word missing the vowels. What word is it if you are told that it refers to a sport?

T _ N N _ S

It is fairly easy to figure out that the word is TENNIS. Now, look at the following word, which is missing the consonants. It refers to someone who likes to go on trips.

_ _ A _ E _ E _

The answer is TRAVELER. Identifying the word this time is much more difficult for most of us because of this principle, called, technically, information entropy. Although it has a broader technical definition, in the case of such puzzles it allows us to understand concretely that consonants carry more information than vowels.

English has 21 letter consonants but only five (sometimes six) letter vowels. Because there are fewer vowels, they appear more frequently in word construction, offering very little in terms of information load, as the communications engineer Claude Shannon called it in his classic 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," in which he quantified how much information a message carries based on its unpredictability—the less predictable something is, the more information it carries. In this framework, consonants have high entropy (high information load), whereas vowels have low entropy (low information load). If the consonants are removed, a word becomes a mystery; if the vowels are removed, it is a fairly easy task to reconstruct it.

Vowels also have information value, as can be seen in those words that are made up only of vowels or are vowel-heavy, such as audio and queue. But these are rare.

At the purely phonetic level, vowels can be seen to have a “pronunciation-smoothing” function. If we try to pronounce a string of consonants, such as NXT (next) or BLDG (building), our mouth jams up. Without vowels, there is almost no continuous airflow. They allow the transition from consonant to consonant (or cluster of consonants) to flow smoothly. This function can also be assumed by liquid consonants (R and L), but, by and large, it falls upon the vowels to allow for unobstructed airflow to occur during speech.

In sum, consonants provide greater information about lexical identity than vowels do. In "Wheel of Fortune," the fact that vowels are highly predictable and appear in almost every word, giving them away for free would make the puzzles too easy to solve.

Example

In the puzzles here, you are given words missing the consonants, thus reversing the rules of "Wheel of Fortune." As in the game, however, you are given a clue as to its meaning:

Appliance:

_ E _ _ I _ E _ A _ O _

The answer is REFRIGERATOR. As you may have experienced, the effort to identify the word is rather substantial. As examples such as this imply, our brain seems to have a “consonant bias,” as posited by the information entropy principle. The clues used here are intentionally generic or tricky. This is meant to emphasize how difficult it is to identify words missing the consonants, especially in the absence of clues that do not zero in concretely on their meanings.

Puzzles

1. A place of higher education

U _ I _ E _ _ I _ _

2. A spice

_ I _ _ A _ O _

3. Handheld know-it-all

_ _ A _ _ _ _ O _ E

4. Colossal

_ I _ A _ I _

5. A monster

_ O _ _ I _ _ A

6. Contemporaneity

_ O _ E _ _ I _ _

7. Proof

_ E _ O _ _ _ _ A _ I O _

8. Dorothea Lange’s art

_ _ O _ O _ _ A _ _ _

9. Input provider

_ E _ _ O A _ _

10. Synthetic lookalike

_ E E _ _ A _ E

Answers

  1. University
  2. Cinnamon
  3. Smartphone
  4. Titanic
  5. Godzilla
  6. Modernity
  7. Demonstration
  8. Photography
  9. Keyboard
  10. Deepfake

item.title: Is Your Car’s “Face” Sad, Angry, Imposing, or Friendly?
item.description:
Play

Is Your Car’s “Face” Sad, Angry, Imposing, or Friendly?

Auto designers attract eyeballs by playing with visual psychology.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Our brain/minds play at seeing faces on cars.
  • Seeing a car’s “face” is like seeing the Man in the Moon.
  • Culture shapes the patterns we recognize, as different societies see different figures in the moon.

When you look at your car, does it stare back? And what expression does it seem to hold? These two questions are surprisingly strange because a car is made of metal, glass, and plastic, and it cannot stare. A car cannot have an expression because a facial expression communicates emotions, and only animals—especially mammals like us humans—have an inner life that can be read on a face.

A face takes on the outward sign of what is going on inside. A face can look happy and expectant. This is the wide-eyed, open, inviting, and smiling “play face” that needs no translation anywhere in the world. We know when a kid is ready to play, wondering what’s next. At the opposite end of the spectrum, a human face can look angry and fearful, and this is one of the most complicated expressions. When the eyebrows pull together and draw downward, observers interpret anger. Add eyebrows turned up at the corner, and we see how the face registers fear. This “blended” expression is also universally and wordlessly understood.

In fact, the human face can explicitly communicate a range of subtle states of mind that others read. With sadness, of course, the brows invert, and the eyelids droop. But more subtly and with more complexity, a sad face can project chagrin or wistfulness, various species of regret, or longing. A face will register shock but can show the effect of more complicated internal turmoil, such as disbelieving shock—this can’t be happening! We know a patient look when we see it, and we know when the patient look turns to exasperation. By looking at a face, we know when a person is confused, bored, at wit’s end, awestruck, disgusted, delighted, on-the-muscle, desirous, or feeling guilty. Here, there, and everywhere on the planet we get faces.

But Back to Cars

But back to car designs. Cars don’t have faces—not the way that people or poodles have faces. But automobile body designers play with design features that look anthropomorphized and expressive. Car designers have specific expressions in mind when they blueprint cars that appear to be looking back at us in specific, emotionally expressive ways. We’re happy to be so regarded, in fact, and will be drawn to those looks in car showrooms.

Our brain/minds play at seeing faces on cars.
Source: Buick Invicta / Image courtesy Jacob Frey 4A via Wikimedia / CC By 2.0

I will get to the how and why below, but for now, here are a few examples. Let me start with a memory of a snazzy family car, a 1959 Buick that sported “delta wing” tail fins, the sheet metal reminiscent of rocket ships or fighter jets. Red taillights looked like flaming rocket exhausts. These identifiable flying objects were on our minds at the peak of the Cold War. Our model was white with a red interior—as I said, snazzy.

But it was what was up front that really counted. First, the dual headlights, shaped like eyes tipped inward— “canted” as the designers described them—to communicate incisiveness. Next, and you will not see this feature on today’s aerodynamically slick autos, the heavy chrome strips above looked like furrowed eyebrows deployed in concentration, or perhaps, wrath. Then below, the grille that ran the car’s full width, was easy to interpret as teeth. The grin looked feral, close to a snarl.

This car looked ready to eat up the road.

Even More Aggressive Faces

This aggressive look sharply contrasted earlier styles. After 15 years of Depression and war, Americans had needed to look at a friendly face. For instance, in 1950, the Buick Roadmaster had seemed out-and-out goofy. Nicknamed “the buck-toothed Buick,” with its massive intake grille (a kind of mouth), and a hood ornament for a nose, this car featured a comical overbite. Droopy eye-headlights amplified the amusing effect.

But after 1959, Cold War-era cars would come to look more aggressive. The hungry looking third-generation Chevrolet Corvette from 1969, for instance, was nicknamed the Mako Shark—its headlights slung low and to the side of gaping jaws, and its hood designed with gliding predatory curves. Engineer-artists have designed today’s eighth generation Corvette models to look even fiercer by including angled, upsweeping anime headlights and a massive manga jawline.

How Cars Are Like the Man in the Moon

Now, for the visual psychology of these designs, we look not to Detroit but to outer space. For several nights each month the night sky treats us to a familiar illusion. Look at a detailed photo of our orbiting moon and you will see only an intricate tracery of rimmed impact craters and smooth “seas.” But stare upward on a moonlit night and your brain/mind will make sense of the random patterns by understanding them as the wryly smiling Man in the Moon. Our visual cortexes have cataloged a category for smiling faces.

Not all Earthlings register this effect as we do in North America. But we all interpret random patterns that culture prepares us to see. In East Asia, a Moon-Rabbit appears. In Australia, where the moon is upside down from our northern and western viewpoint, Australians see St. George slaying his dragon.

The same process allowed Hamlet and Polonius to argue whether clouds looked like camels or weasels, early astronomers to intuit canals on Mars, and the faithful to see angels appear on slices of French toast. Even now we might see mimetolithic trolls on sheer rock façades and wizened Ent-like men in tree bark patterns.

Why Do We See What We don’t See?

We infuse these inanimate objects with personality through a process that psychologists since the mid-nineteenth century have called pareidolia. Because our mind/brains strive to avoid ambiguity and randomness, they play at seeing an object where one does not really exist.

Turn your search engine toward “pareidolia” and you’ll have no trouble detecting cartoon pigs on the coats of palominos, Valkyries in cowlicks, an outraged imp in a sectioned green pepper, a pelvis in a Rorschach blot, or Mother Theresa’s face on a cinnamon bun.

Or, indeed, you will find agreeable connection to a sad, goofy, friendly, or imposing face on a car’s front end.

item.title: An Analysis of the Film "You Can See Everything"
item.description:
Authenticity

An Analysis of the Film "You Can See Everything"

Elizabeth Holmes's responses to questioning may suggest appeasement.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Apparent agreeableness can invite escalating intrusions rather than signal genuine consent.
  • Believing we uniquely understand someone can lead us to override their wishes and autonomy.
  • The film may reveal others’ appropriation of Holmes’s identity more than her authentic self.
Source: A24

In the trailer for "You Can See Everything," Nathan Fielder positions himself inches from Elizabeth Holmes’s face and asks whether she is telling the truth. Her eyebrows are raised, her eyes wide, and her smile eerily fixed. The expression is disturbing in isolation. But in the film, Fielder returns to the question of her honesty again and again, often at the same invasive distance. Holmes continues smiling and nodding, maintaining that she has never lied while offering remarkably little resistance to his relentless questioning. What initially looked like an unnatural expression begins to resemble an attempt to appease the man confronting her.

As a psychologist and author of the forthcoming book Being Seen, I was particularly interested in a documentary that promised such intimate access to one of the most scrutinized women in America. What interested me was how the people surrounding Holmes might influence what we actually get to see of her.

Why Is Holmes So Agreeable?

This is not a diagnosis, but Holmes’s persistent smile brings to mind fawning, a response in which someone attempts to appease a person they experience as threatening or overpowering. Rather than objecting or withdrawing, they become extremely agreeable, anticipate what the other person wants, and try to avoid further confrontation. Someone may continue smiling even when the encounter has become deeply uncomfortable.

Holmes’s apparent submissiveness in the film may have a longer history. Although she founded and controlled Theranos, a company once valued in the billions, she testified during her trial that her former romantic and business partner, Sunny Balwani, tried to control her appearance and daily life and subjected her to emotional and sexual abuse. Balwani denied the allegations. Watching Holmes accommodate Fielder’s increasingly intrusive questioning raises the possibility that appeasing a domineering person is a familiar way of relating for her.

Billy Evans, Holmes’s current partner, has taken charge of much of her public image while she is incarcerated. Holmes has given him power of attorney, and he writes social-media posts in her name and has even created an artificial intelligence (AI) likeness of her. He says he often doesn’t consult her because he already knows what she wants. His confidence extends to how he interprets her behavior. When Fielder challenges Holmes’s explanations, Evans suggests that she simply thinks differently. What others see as contradictions, he regards as evidence of her unusual mind. His belief in her exceptionalism also gives him a special place in her life: He is the one who understands what others cannot.

Fielder claims a different kind of authority over Holmes. He has built his career around creating social encounters that become almost unbearable to watch, yet Holmes and Evans chose him to make their documentary. Evans was familiar with his work, while Holmes apparently knew little about it. When Fielder asks why they selected him, he receives no clear answer. Once inside their home, he controls the questions, the physical proximity, and ultimately what audiences see. His investigation becomes an increasingly elaborate production, often at Holmes’s expense. She continues to engage with him, smiling through questions that might make other people angry or defensive.

Amanda Seyfried assumes another kind of authority. Having portrayed Holmes in The Dropout, she joins the documentary after Holmes enters prison, reenacting conversations reconstructed from Fielder’s recollections. Soon she is challenging Evans and questioning his influence on Holmes. Seyfried resembles an understudy finally called to play the leading role, except that the woman she replaces has not given up her part. Having inhabited her character, she behaves as though she has acquired special insight into the real woman, even her choice of partner.

How Appeasement Can Invite Increasing Intrusions on Identity

Holmes's extraordinary pliability seems to invite increasingly intrusive behavior. Fielder positions himself inches from her face and repeatedly questions her honesty while she smiles and continues to engage with him. Evans, whose authority she has formally granted, becomes so confident in his understanding of her that he sees little reason to ask what she wants before speaking in her name. While Holmes is in prison, Seyfried steps into her place, reenacting private conversations reconstructed from Fielder’s memory. She goes beyond playing Holmes, however, by insisting that the real woman should leave Evans. What begins with someone taking liberties during a conversation progresses to others assuming the authority to speak for Holmes and eventually to become her. Each seems convinced that their particular understanding of Holmes entitles them to take it further.

Being the person who truly understands someone can be deeply gratifying. It can make us feel perceptive, indispensable, or uniquely trusted. Over time, we may become attached to that position and increasingly reluctant to question our understanding. We explain away behavior that doesn't fit our picture, assume we know what another person wants, or interpret their agreement as confirmation that we were right all along. Even their silence can reinforce our certainty. The more invested we become in our understanding of someone, the less room we may leave for them to surprise us, disagree with us, or reveal parts of themselves we never anticipated.

I left the theater feeling far more empathy for Holmes than I expected. Her accommodating manner, which initially seemed almost artificial, began to resemble an attempt to appease people who were taking increasing liberties with her. What troubled me was how confidently those around her assumed the authority to question, protect, interpret, and eventually impersonate her. Holmes had invited some of this attention and granted some of this authority, yet the boundaries kept shifting. The irony of "You Can See Everything" is that we witness this gradual appropriation of Holmes's identity in plain sight, even as our attention remains fixed on the question of who she really is.

item.title: Why the Push for High Performance Backfires and What Helps
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Why the Push for High Performance Backfires and What Helps

It’s not just you. Your capacity is shaped by the conditions around you.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Conditions beyond your control can erode capacity, making it harder to execute at the level you are used to.
  • Stress and insufficient support can disrupt your ability to think clearly, plan, and follow through.
  • When you fall short, address what is under your control and acknowledge what is not, without shame.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Have you ever sat down to begin a task, only to feel as if all the motivation immediately left your body? I often find myself saying, “I want to do this,” but for some reason, I can’t.

I used to associate high performance with operating from a consistent level of high capacity. I had an identity around doing as much as possible, as quickly as possible. In recent years, I have come to accept that an approach I once considered an advantage, one that was celebrated and reinforced in every academic or work setting I entered, became maladaptive over time.

When I first started struggling with tasks, my response was to push harder, which only made it worse. I felt like Humpty Dumpty. The old version of me who seemingly used to do it all had fallen off a wall. No matter what I tried, I wasn’t going back to that way of functioning. I thought about quitting my job. I wondered why no one else seemed to be struggling. Now I know that many are, and somehow, that simultaneously makes it better and scarier. Better in that I’m not alone, but scarier in that no one holds the secret to reset. We have to go through this, and grow through this, one step at a time. Together, we are learning how to walk (and work) differently.

How Stress Affects Our Capacity

We may be carrying a physical, emotional, or cognitive load that is invisible to others, and perhaps even ourselves. This could be anything from tension in our bodies and unresolved or suppressed emotions to an open loop of tasks. Each of these can affect our capacity in any given moment and our ability to meet expectations or fulfill what is being asked of us.

In my search a few years back for answers to why I suddenly found it so difficult to plan, organize, and see tasks through, I stumbled across executive function, a set of processes that help us engage in goal-directed behavior such as planning, making decisions, initiating and seeing tasks through, and regulating our emotions.

When we experience a stressor, ideally, the part of our brain that controls executive function (the prefrontal cortex) responds. However, the amygdala, associated with a fear (fight, flight, freeze) response, can overpower or shortcut the prefrontal cortex. When this happens, we are more likely to react impulsively. This is why we often find it difficult to engage in the coping behaviors we know would be most helpful.

Even the most basic tasks may feel impossible. It’s hard to think clearly, make decisions, or be kind to ourselves. All we can see is what we haven’t done.

Planning becomes difficult because it takes effort and energy. Our brains may default to habits and behaviors associated with protecting us from danger, including shutting down. Even when we want to follow advice that feels aligned for us, it’s hard because we lack the capacity, support, or resources.

Often it isn’t until the perceived threat or pressure is eased that our capacity returns.

Shame Is a Quick Fix With a Hidden Cost

Where could I go to hide from myself? If I am shaming myself, I’m not going to ask for help; I’m not going to change what I can; I’m simply going to conclude that I’m not enough.

This is how I end up feeling stuck.

When we have internalized high expectations and are not able to meet them, we see ourselves as the problem. We don’t have a clear, direct way to attribute it to the environment, and even if we did, we don’t control that. So we try to control what we can by shaming ourselves toward greater productivity and, thus, worthiness and acceptance.

Our worth is tied to neither successes nor setbacks. Caring for ourselves means seeing the reality that we are struggling, without seeing ourselves as the struggle. For me, this means fiercely protecting my self-concept by:

  • tuning into what I am experiencing and what I need
  • finding people who can see me for who I am
  • cutting my to-do list down to a grace list (to help me survive this day)
  • saying no to protect my yes
  • advocating for my needs and reality

No one can see what I don’t communicate and advocate for.

Accountability That Accounts for Conditions

When we set out to meet what we believe are reasonable expectations and fall short, we often judge ourselves, believing it is our fault. We rarely consider the larger context, current conditions, or fluctuations of human performance. We hold ourselves to the standards of a should that has never met our reality. We achieve closure by resorting to self-blame, which comes at the cost of the inner trust and safety we need to take risks moving forward. A better approach is to hold ourselves accountable without heaping blame and acknowledge conditions beyond ourselves.

This is a collaborative effort. It begins with leaders proactively providing support, acknowledging gaps in resources, and setting conditions that encourage honesty about one’s capacity and the potential impact of modifying expectations. Without this, sharing one’s true needs can be a liability. If you are your own boss, this is a matter of self-leadership. You must be intentional in creating a culture that will sustain you.

How to Reframe High Performance

The idea of high performance being personified by individuals is short-sighted, as it assumes human capacity is consistent, or worse, ever-expanding. Instead of thinking of individuals as high performers, consider the conditions that foster sustained impact, and take proactive steps to safeguard humanity and replenish capacity. When people break, the culture crumbles.

Leaders can start by being honest about the challenges they are facing, and those being faced by people in their organization. What are they modeling? Are they empowering their people to make decisions and work in a way that is sustainable? Or are they accelerating conditions for burnout? Expecting ever higher levels of performance without adequate support and resources strains the individual and ultimately compromises the organization’s culture and capacity to fulfill its mission.

Whether you lead the culture or work within it, you are not alone. We are all walking through this and figuring it out in real time amidst a rapidly changing world. You do not have to prove yourself or prevent this from ever happening again. The practice is learning to anchor yourself in who you are outside of what you do, and to protect your capacity and preserve your light.

item.title: Your Feelings Are Real. Are They Accurate?
item.description:
Fear

Your Feelings Are Real. Are They Accurate?

Emotions establish that something was experienced, not necessarily what it means.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • A feeling can be entirely real while the conclusion drawn from it is mistaken.
  • Feelings are worth taking seriously but on their own they can't tell us who did what, or why.
  • Respecting feelings means investigating what they signal.

The meeting was heated. I made a statement in order to bring us back to the main issue. All of a sudden, a colleague made a comment about my statement. The comment did not sound collegial or helpful. I felt he was questioning my expertise. I felt uncomfortable. By any HR definition, I had enough to submit a complaint against him, and I had the strongest possible evidence: my feelings. Was I right? Did I need anything more?

Years ago, a professional heavyweight boxer came to see me. Without any doubt, he was better equipped to defend himself than almost anyone who had ever sat in my office.

He came because of spiders.

His fear was so severe that the word alone could set it off. If he heard that someone had seen a spider in the building next door, his heart would race, he would start to sweat, and everything in him wanted to get out. Needless to mention, we met in a country where spiders pose almost no danger to anyone.

I have thought about him often over the years, because his case raises a question much bigger than spiders.

Did his fear make spiders dangerous? Of course not. His terror was completely genuine as an experience, but wildly out of proportion as an estimate of risk. It told me a great deal about him: what he had learned, what had happened to him, the associations his nervous system had quietly built over a lifetime. It told me almost nothing about spiders.

That is true of emotions in general. Our feelings don't read the world the way a thermometer reads temperature. They come from appraisals, the quick and mostly automatic judgments we make about what a situation means for us. Those judgments are shaped by temperament, history, culture, mood, and expectation, so every emotion carries news about two things at once: the situation and the person feeling it. When the appraisal is right, emotion is a wonderful guide. Fear spots danger. Anger registers injustice. Discomfort warns that a line has been crossed. When the appraisal is off, we feel fear where there is no danger, jealousy where there was no betrayal, and even a strange calm when we should be alarmed.

Clinicians have a name for one version of this mistake: emotional reasoning. It is the quiet logic of "I feel anxious, so something must be wrong." We also borrow whatever mood we happen to be in and let it color judgments that have nothing to do with it.

In workplaces, families, and institutions, discomfort is sometimes offered not just as a description of an experience but as proof that someone did something wrong. "What you said made me uncomfortable," we claim, with the unspoken understanding that this settles the matter. But there's a step being skipped. A feeling inside one person can feel like evidence of misconduct by another. But that boxer reminds us that this leap doesn't happen on its own. Discomfort can come from genuine mistreatment. It can also come from a misunderstanding, from an old wound the other person knows nothing about, from different norms colliding, from hearing a truth we didn't want to hear, or simply from difference: an unfamiliar accent, an unpopular opinion, a reasonable disagreement.

This analogy has limits, and people are far more ambiguous than spiders. And unlike a phobia, discomfort in a relationship can be an early sign of harm that hasn't yet shown its shape—harm that builds slowly or depends on who holds power over whom. The feeling, and the explanation we attach to it, are two different things.

I felt uncomfortable. This one short sentence often carries several claims folded together: Something you did caused it. You should have seen it coming. You meant it. And it was wrong. The first is something only the speaker can know, and each claim after it asks for more interpretation and evidence.

I have watched this sentence used as a weapon. A colleague raises a legitimate criticism, or points to a gap in someone's skills, and suddenly the conversation is no longer about the criticism. It is about the discomfort it caused, and now the person who raised it is the one under review. Once that happens, the original concern is rarely heard again, and the reported feeling may be treated as a finding.

That is why treating the feeling as the verdict creates a problem. If discomfort counts as settled proof, the other person has no way to address what actually happened. Subjective experience is still evidence; in medicine we rely on people's reports of pain every day. But on its own, it rarely tells us what another person intended or exactly what took place.

There is a mistake waiting on the other side, and it is just as serious: deciding that feelings are noise, and so "you're just being emotional" counts as an answer. It doesn't. The boxer's fear provided no evidence about spiders, but it was excellent evidence that something in his life needed attention. It was where his treatment began.

Discomfort is often the first sign of mistreatment. People who are being harassed or bullied may feel uneasy long before they can name the pattern. Brush feelings aside and you throw away exactly the signal that protects people. And when someone's accurate perceptions are dismissed again and again, especially as part of a broader pattern of control, that dismissal can do lasting damage of its own.

Perhaps the wiser path is to reject both errors: Feelings are not verdicts, and they are not noise. They are testimony from a witness who may be entirely sincere and whose report may matter enormously, but whose interpretation can still be incomplete or mistaken.

My boxer, by the way, recovered—but not because anyone told him his fear was silly. It wasn't silly; it was agony. He got better because we took his suffering seriously while gently reshaping his sense of danger against reality. In our last meeting, I told him that the next time he saw a spider, he might consider how terrified that little spider must be to see a giant like him. He laughed.

I think that is what all our emotions deserve: respect as experiences, attention as signals, and a careful look before we treat what they suggest as fact.

A final note: My colleague was right. My statement did not carry enough substance to suggest I was talking as an expert.
